top.line: A guided tour of the Mesa Ranch observation desk
top.para: The Mesa Ranch desk turns Francesco Marconi's INMA deck into seventeen pages on synthetic records: the argument, the system, the record and five graphs. Every page shares a frame of menu, page and evidence panel. The tour explains what each page shows, what to click and what it proves, and how to rebuild it.

in-short.line: Seventeen pages, one frame, all synthetic and rebuildable
in-short.para: The argument covers proprietary observation and delta science. The system has four actors, an atlas of 78 event types and an ontology of six entities. The record has seventeen observations, one AI cycle, three queues and a tracker. Five graphs show the same knowledge. Clone it with the read key.

how.line: Every page shares one frame: menu, page, evidence panel
how.para: The vault is published with its read key and opens as its own app. The menu on the left follows the deck in five groups; the page sits in the middle; clicking a marker, record, observation, family, entity or node opens its details and evidence on the right. All names and records are synthetic.

argument.line: Delta science shows what changed, backed by the record
argument.para: The cover introduces 12 families, 78 event types, 16 records and 17 observations. The advantage page counts 13 sources watched, 78 event types recognised and seven comparisons connected. Delta science shows ranch land in November 2025 against a power station and three data halls in October 2026, with clickable permits, minutes, deeds and agreements.

system.line: An atlas of 78 event types drives the method
system.para: Four actors are mapped: power provider, developer, local government and residents. The atlas groups 78 event types into twelve families, each with a definition and observable signal; the deck showed only 12, and most are unseen yet. The ontology has six entities and relationships, following the rule that an event changes a state or relationship.

record.line: One AI cycle catches a schedule slip by comparison
record.para: Seventeen observations sit on a timeline with tags and evidence. The workflow follows R14: phase one slips from the second half of 2027 to the first half of 2028, a journalist checks it, an alert goes out and O15 is recorded. Three queues direct monitoring, investigation and publishing; the tracker covers jobs and water questions.

graphs.line: Five graphs show the same knowledge in five shapes
graphs.para: The fractal graph opens level by level from the question to records. Rings show every level at once, revealing that few branches carry the news. The knowledge graph replays relationships over time, including the ownership change. Records to observations draws the evidence, and the delta chain arcs each observation to its earlier comparison.

yours.line: Clone the vault and rebuild it for your beat
yours.para: The last page follows the deck's four steps: choose a question, map the system, define its events, keep observing. To build your own, clone the vault, replace the families, entities, records and question in tools/build_data.py and run the three scripts. The real work is defining each event and its signal.

limits.line: Synthetic records, no live watching, not Marconi's endorsed work
limits.para: Every name and record is invented, and the desk runs the method on fixed records rather than watching anything live. The deck shows 12 of 78 event types; the rest of the atlas is the site's own. It is a reading of Marconi's public slides, not his work and not endorsed by him.

sources.line: Sources: the published vault and the earlier article
sources.para: Written at my request on 15 October 2026 after seeing the vault, by this site's agent. Screenshots show the vault as published that day. The idea and method are in When journalism becomes intelligence, built, which links Francesco Marconi's slides and reporting on the real project they drew on.
